newsitem.title: UK: Euro Eurobonds - phonetically awkward but true. [CORRECTED 14:00 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Euro Eurobonds - phonetically awkward but true. [CORRECTED 14:00 GMT]

text.p: The tongue-twisting euro Eurobond sector -- international bonds denominated in the future European currency -- has had to be born without a more suitable name as market changes outpaced philology.

Cliff Dammers, secretary general of the International Primary Market Association, said the problem had been informally discussed, but it seems some proposals that have popped up have little chance of winning wide recognition.
"I refuse to call it a euro Euro' or a yo-yo bond' as some people have called it which has got to be the ugliest name I've ever heard," he said.
He said there was sentiment in favour of calling Eurobonds international bonds. "That's the best I've heard, although its not very catchy."
"Euro Eurobond is definitely a bit of a mouthful and rather odd," a syndicate official at a U.S. bank said. "I'm sure it'll be called something else, but for now, no one knows what."
But others say the name will be hard to replace.
"You can't teach an old dog new tricks," another syndicate manager said. "Euro Eurobond is fine by me."
Calling Eurobonds Xenobonds, from the ancient Greek Xeno meaning foreign, has its fans too.
Dammers said the Xenobond idea had been "kicking around for about 20 years".
But many traders said Xenobonds linguistically associate with xenophobia which could inhibit some potential investors.
The market needs to adopt a new name because post-EMU, euro bonds and Eurobonds will be markedly different instruments while being pronounced identically.
Euro bonds will be domestic issues for EMU member countries, while Eurobonds are international offerings.
Two Eurobond transactions launched this month illustrated the problem.
Both contain clauses allowing them to be redenominated into euros from January 1, 1999, when the single currency is expected to come into effect in the third stage of monetary union.
The first was from Austria in French francs via joint lead managers CDC and J.P. Morgan and the second for the European Investment Bank in guilders via ABN AMRO Hoare Govett.
Both have maturities well beyond key EMU dates of 1999 and 2002.
Nonetheless, whatever the confusion over names, business will go on as usual in the sector, traders said. "A rose will still be a rose by any other name," one trader said.
